ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to Jeff Simpson of The Globe and Mail the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) declared that acid rain represented the litmus test of Canada-U.S. relations. If so, the Americans have flunked the test, and so by implication has the Prime Minister. His Government's strategy of less rhetoric, reduced lobbying, fewer public complaints, and the special envoys' process produced meagre results-more U.S. research and a statement by the President that acid rain was indeed a transboundary problem.
Unfortunately, the Prime Minister's policy also disheartened Canada's congressional allies. Every time they sought to get something going, the Reaganites could respond that even the Canadians accepted the administration's approach.
The Prime Minister now says Congress is at fault for not passing acid rain control legislation. Yet his Government's policy hurt congressional efforts.
This toughening reflects the political reality that nothing further can be gained from the administration. President Reagan is already history. The rhetoric also reflects the need to deflect criticism back home that the close relations with President Reagan led Canada up a deadend street.
What a sham, Mr. Speaker.

ABORTION
subsubtopic: CHARTER OF RIGHTS-PROTECTION OF UNBORN CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, "The testimony of modern science and technology asserts most
emphatically a truth that was not so certain even 20 years ago, namely, that from the moment of conception everything is present for the gradual development of a unique human person; nothing is added by the mother or any other source".
This sentence is taken from an open letter to Members of Parliament from His Excellency the Bishop of Alexandria-Cornwall. He goes on to say: "With this present scientific knowledge and the assurance of our Christian faith my request to you", that is, Members of Parliament, "is to enshrine the right to life from the moment of conception in law and in our Charter of Human Rights ..."
I urge the Government and all Members to heed this message from the Bishop.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO DEPORTATION OF REFUGEE STATUS CLAIMANTS TO EL SALVADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, telegrams from Canadians are demanding that the Government stop its new program of trying to railroad Salvadoran refugee claimants back to El Salvador.
Recently a Salvadoran trade unionist who had been imprisoned and tortured for his union work there, lost his plea for refugee status in Canada and was to be deported to El Salvador until Amnesty International intervened to ensure that his appeal is heard before he leaves Canada. On the record documented by the American Civil Liberties Union and the General Accounting Office of the U.S. Congress, he has good reason to fear persecution if forced back to El Salvador.
Another Salvadoran whose bus driver brother was murdered by the Salvadoran Army, fled rather than be conscripted by that same army to kill his neighbours. Here he was imprisoned so that he was unable to get a lawyer to help his case, and in discouragement withdrew his refugee claim. Fortunately, his case will be reviewed by the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, since in El Salvador he is under death squad threat.
Is this the purpose for which the Government recently dumped some of the best qualified members of the Refugee Status Advisory Committee, to intimidate the rest into sending Salvadorans back to death squads?

April 27, 1988

POLITICAL PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most Canadians are in favour of free trade. I would like to point out the visit my Prime Minister is paying to Washington today. Three cheers to Brian Mulroney for his tenacity and his efforts to strengthen bilateral trade with our southern neighbour!
Liberals and New Democrats, the end is near. You have only one thing left to do: pay tribute to our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney, who is leading our country so brilliantly. He is a very talented statesman whom we are pleased to follow and support. I thank the residents of the riding of La Prairie for giving me the chance to live such moments in this House.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, there is a postscript to this comment. Canadians are living through a time of glory, rejoicing and pride, all because of the Conservatives in the country.
Victory in Manitoba! Congratulations! And even at the risk of repeating myself, I say that Canada has the greatest Prime Minister ever elected.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: HISTORIC EVENTS
HISTORIC EVENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday with pride and joy I joined approximately 6,000 Montrealers in song and dance to celebrate Israel's fortieth birthday.
Growing from the ashes of the Holocaust, that blot on the collective memory of mankind, this state has settled Jewish refugees from over 75 nations of the world, renewed the land, planted trees, built roads, housing, industry, set up hospitals and health services, and put in place a modern democracy founded on the basic values of traditional Jewish culture, respect for learning, justice and charity.
Yet even with these successes no nation is whole without peace. This fledgling state has withstood assaults from its Arab neighbours, and survived continuous hostility and a condition of quasi-war ever since it was born.
Since its founding days Israel has fought five wars for survival, and its citizens still face an ongoing difficult security situation.
While the present unrest concerns us all, we must not give up hope. We must persevere in our support for peace in the
region, a peace which history has yet to record for Israel and its Arab-Palestinian neighbours, a peace negotiated directly by Israel and the Palestinians, a peace that includes full recognition of Israel by her neighbours and acceptance of her right to secure borders.
Surely Israel and the Palestinians deserve such fundamental democratic rights as we hold so dear here in Canada.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: WELFARE
WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one accomplishment in which this Government can take pride, it is the significant reduction in poverty levels since it took office.
The National Council of Welfare, in its recent publication "Poverty Profile 1988", says that, in our first two years in office, the poverty rate decreased from 17.3 per cent to 14.9 per cent. Some 525,000 individuals were removed from the ranks of the poor between 1984 and 1986 alone.
The real success story has been the reduction in poverty among Canada's elderly. Our prime area of concern is now to repeat this success for families headed by single women.
The economic and social policies of the Conservative Government have been unparalleled when it comes to alleviating hardship amongst the less well off.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: DISARMAMENT
DISARMAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year, prompted by growing public concern about the export of arms and military related goods from Canada, I called upon the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to establish a public commission of inquiry to undertake a thorough and careful study of Canada's military export policies and practices. Unfortunately, the Minister failed to establish such a commission of inquiry. However, he has now agreed to set up a technical working group, as recommended recently by the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security, to examine the feasibility of an arms register. This is an encouraging and timely development.
While I welcome the Minister's decision, I must protest his Department's failure to invite representatives of disarmament groups, particularly Ernie Regehr, of Project Ploughshares, who has skilfully and eloquently promoted a need for an arms register for many years, to attend the inaugural meeting of the working group.
April 27, 1988

Unless the Minister broadens the representation of this group to include disarmament organizations, the group's credibility is put seriously in question.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: THE DISABLED AND THE HANDICAPPED
THE DISABLED AND THE HANDICAPPED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians who live with mental or physical disability face many challenges that are, in and of themselves, hard enough to overcome. If, on top of that, you happen to be a native Canadian, the barriers can be truly awesome.
In 1981 a special parliamentary committee recommended a series of steps to help disabled natives lead independent and dignified lives. In 1985 those recommendations in respect of native Canadians were endorsed a second time, in the parliamentary committee report "Equality for All".
To date, however, there is little indication from either native or non-native sources that any significant progress has been made.
In the initial report of the Committee on the Disabled, brought down exactly one year ago, I advised the House that the Department of Indian Affairs had no services for disabled natives, had no future plans for such programs, and did not consider disability prevention to be an issue of concern.
It will come as no surprise, therefore, that the Parliamentary Committee on the Status of Disabled Persons intends to investigate this situation.

[ Translation]

SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

April 27, 1988

President on the line, and state Canada's position on acid rain clearly and unequivocally on behalf of people north of the 49th parallel who now consider this to be the most important issue of our neighbourship with the United States?

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: UNITED STATES POLICY ON NITROGEN OXIDE EMISSIONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: UNITED STATES POLICY ON NITROGEN OXIDE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary of State for External Affairs hopefully is aware, and Canadians today learned with dismay, that the U.S. negotiators in Geneva have rejected Canada's demand that a planned increase in the United States emissions of nitrogen oxide, which is the key ingredient of acid rain, would only be permitted and should only be permitted if this increase did not result in more pollution for Canada. That was Canada's demand which American negotiators have rejected.
Will the Secretary of State tell us whether the Prime Minister today in Washington will insist that the President reverse this short-sighted and disastrous policy announced in Geneva today, because it really means that the United States still plans to increase, and not decrease, the acid rain pollution of our lakes, forests, rivers, and our environment. Did the Prime Minister know the President was going to allow this to happen by way of his negotiators in Geneva on the very day he was addressing the United States Congress?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subtopic: UNITED STATES POLICY ON NITROGEN OXIDE EMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one-third of the acid rain that wreaks havoc on the Canadian environment comes from nitrogen oxide. About two-thirds of that NOx comes from the United States. Clearly, the Prime Minister will be raising that dimension of the problem with the President during his private and public meetings.
The position of Canada has always been clear in Geneva at successive meetings of our top officials there. We oppose any American position that has been on the table at successive meetings that would have the effect of increasing NOx emissions from such a source. We have opposed it in the past, we oppose it now, and we will oppose it at future meetings. The Prime Minister of Canada will be expressing his opposition in the most unqualified terms in Washington today and tomorrow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be an unfortunate coincidence for the Canadian Government and the Prime Minister of Canada that, on the very day he addresses the U.S. Congress, American negotiators in Geneva announce a decision that is very negative for Canada.
Now that the Prime Minister has discovered the existence of the U.S. Congress, will he show some firmness in his speech today before Congress or is he going to soften his position so as not to compromise the passage of his free trade agreement with the United States? Are we heading towards free trade in acid rain?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subtopic: QUERY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL SHOW FIRMNESS IN SPEECH TO UNITED STATES CONGRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really am puzzled. The Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition attaches a great deal of symbolic importance to the fact that there is a meeting in Geneva today when the Prime Minister of Canada is in Washington. The negotiators from 34 countries have been meeting almost non-stop for the last year and a half, or two years.
The meeting in Geneva is important, but it is no more important than the meetings held in February or in November, or those that will be held in future months. We are not completing a protocol in Geneva this week. Indeed, I would doubt whether enough progress will be made by the international community to make it possible to sign such an Accord by next October, which was the original deadline.
In any event, the Prime Minister of Canada, unlike the Prime Minister of the day in 1977, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, will be expressing, on the floor of Congress, Canadian concerns in very unqualified terms. This is in sharp contrast to the situation that prevailed when the Liberal Party of Canada was in power. It would not raise the subject on the floor of the House of Commons, let alone on the floor of Congress in Washington.

speechtext:
How sweet it is, Mr. Speaker.
I have a supplementary question for the Minister of the Environment. He has just said how the Prime Minister will be taking tough stands and strengthening his rhetoric with the President. It was not so long ago that in this House the Prime Minister was castigating a Member of the U.S. Congress who had the nerve to suggest that the Canadian Prime Minister and the Canadian administration were selling out on acid rain.
Why has the Prime Minister now changed his tune? Will he retract or repudiate those statements he made in this House when he was saying that it was wrong for U.S. Congressmen to be asking for a Clean Air Act and that they should go along with the Reagan plan?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subtopic: POSITION OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister said no such thing. The Government of Canada should be judged by its actions and those actions are a heck of a lot tougher against acid rain than those taken by any previous Government. We have slashed acid rain-causing emissions from Canadian sources by 50 per cent and that will take effect by 1994, based on levels that prevailed in 1980, as far as sulphur dioxide is concerned.
We have instituted the toughest anti-NOx program in the world. When we took office in September of 1984, emission controls in Canada for nitrogen oxide were only one-third as strict as those that prevailed in the United States, greatly undermining our capacity as a country to point the finger at Washington for stronger measures. Now we have slashed allowable emissions by 60 per cent for light cars and trucks, and by 50 per cent for heavy-duty vehicles. That control program is the toughest in the world. We should be judged by our actions, and our actions have been very strong.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. Last week, the Prime Minister's office published the list of ministerial task forces, which no longer includes the Montreal Region Development Committee. A spokesman for the Prime Minister confirmed this unfortunate state of affairs.
Today, however, according to the media, the Minister's spokesman said the Committee still exists. Who is telling the truth?

subtopic: REGIONAL INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION
subsubtopic: QUERY WHETHER MONTREAL REGION ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE STILL EXISTS

The sub-committee of the Economic Development Committee for the Montreal region was created at the same time as the Montreal Region Advisory Committee, so that appropriate recommendations could be made, based on information provided by the Advisory Committee.
Subsequently, the Advisory Committee's recommendations were considered and largely agreed to by the ministerial task force, and these recommendations were referred to the respective departments, while the Economic Development Committee, which is in charge of these matters, took over the responsability.
So we are talking about an ad hoc committee, a subcommittee like many other committees that still exist today and are not on the list. This Committee did a lot of work during the time it was working with the Advisory Committee, which has submitted its report. The report has been approved and its implementation is in progress.

April 27, 1988

QUERY WHY GOVERNMENT IGNORED PICARD REPORT RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, according to officials at the office of the Mayor of Montreal, the Committee still exists. However, if I understand correctly, the Minister confirmed today that the Committee is no longer active.
My second question is very straightforward: According to the office of the Mayor of Montreal, the Picard Report made some very concrete and practical suggestions but the federal Government completely ignored them. Why?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Sub-Committee on Economic Development of the Montreal region, which reported to the Cabinet Committee on Economic Development, may be asked to meet at any time, if this is judged to be appropriate. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows perfectly well that the people of Montreal did not like the Government's response in this respect and more specifically, the Picard Report recommended that the federal Government support the Vieux-Port, the Space Agency and a number of projects concerning the region's infrastructure. speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: FEDERAL GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It has to do with the fact that last January the Canadian Government agreed to trade northern cod just to get the Government of France to the bargaining table on the boundary dispute over St. Pierre and Miquelon.
Now after some theatrics by the fishermen and some politicians of St. Pierre, the Government is offering to go to non-binding mediation to give some more fish to the St. Pierre fishermen, and also, we hear, to metropolitan France, just to get them talking about fish again.
Why has the Government refused, or is no longer continuing to keep together the two issues of the boundary dispute and the issue of fishing in Canadian waters? Can the Minister assure the House that there will be no concessions to the French Government unless it agrees to submit the boundary dispute to third party arbitration?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade
subtopic: FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman does not seem to understand the process that has been under way now for several years. That is a process in which the Government of Canada is most anxious to settle the question of the territorial boundaries of
Oral Questions
St. Pierre and Miquelon. It can only be settled by an international arbitration, or by the International Court because the two parties cannot otherwise agree. We believe it is the duty of both to go to an international adjudication on this.
In the same manner as France and Great Britain went to international arbitration on the question of the Channel Islands, so should France now agree to go with us.
Unfortunately, France is trying to tie to that and make a condition of it agreeing to go to arbitration on that question, the settlement of the issue of what quotas it should receive under the 1972 treaty in Canadian waters for the next three years or so while the matter goes to arbitration. France has been making that a condition, and that is what the process has been about for the last several years.
The Government has taken a firm position. We have closed our ports to French vessels because of their overfishing in 3PS. We will continue on that course. We will take a firm and reasonable stand meeting our international obligations, but trying to get these issues settled in a way that will protect the fishermen of Atlantic Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Harris (St. John's East) moved:
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-103 be amended in Clause 7
(a)	by striking out line 14 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"the order, any area in Atlantic Canada, which may be a sub-region in a province,"
(b)	by striking out line 18 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"employment by means of pilot projects and multi-year comprehensive area development strategies and action plans and other means as necessary."
He said: Mr. Speaker, as was just indicated, there are a series of amendments to the Bill that I have proposed as a member of the legislative committee. A number of other amendments were proposed in committee which were defeated, including Motion No. 1 which referred to the requirement by the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency to have, as one of its advisory boards, an advisory board to advise the agency on programs with specific relation to women in business. As Mr. Speaker has just ruled, it can no longer be debated in this House.
The motion presently before the House provides for an amendment to Clause No. 7. Clause No. 7 provides for special areas to be designated by the Minister within the Atlantic provinces, special areas for which special rules may be able to govern. If we look at the provisions in the legislation with respect to special areas, we will see that the Minister has the power to designate special areas in the Atlantic region. The Bill says:
-a designated area, for the period set out in the order, any area in Atlantic Canada where, in the opinion of the Minister, exceptional circumstances provide opportunity for locally based improvements in productive employment.
The motion provides to amend that particular clause as follows to clarify so that it will be beyond any doubt that those areas may be "a sub-region in a province". It need not be an entire province. It need not be a particular community but it may be as well a sub-region of a province. It would add as well to the end of the clause the following, and would now read:
April 27, 1988

That where, in the opinion of the Minister, exceptional circumstances provide opportunities for locally based improvements in productive employment by means of pilot projects and multi-year comprehensive area development strategies and action plans and other means as necessary.
This motion would amplify and make it clear that these special areas in Atlantic Canada would have opportunities under the agency to have not merely special programs and special rules related to the accessibility to funds under the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, but also support by the agency directly for plans made by community based development groups, such as those presently organized under the Department of Manpower and Immigration. An example of this is the Community Futures Program.
The legislative committee heard representations from organizations such as the Cumberland Community Futures Committee which was quite concerned about the fact that its work, in a sense, mirrors on a community or county basis the community-based or local decision-making that the Minister suggests would be undertaken in Atlantic Canada for development projects. Together, there is a co-operative plan between businesses, communities, municipalities and the federal Government. The comprehensive plans for development will meet local concerns. These organizations are aware of the plans of local communities and of how special programs could be set up to meet the needs of those communities.
In the Province of Newfoundland and certainly in my own riding, there are areas where there are not only special opportunities but also special needs for particular development programs and strategies that are comprehensive in nature. I am thinking in particular of the community of Bell Island in my riding, a once prosperous mining community with a population similar to that of the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon of which we have heard so much lately. This island is less than a mile from the mainland of Newfoundland. Its population has gone down from about 16,000 in the 1960s to somewhat less than 5,000. Job opportunities are very few and special programs are necessary in areas like this.
This legislation would allow a strategy or action plan to be developed for such a region, permitting broadly based initiatives of community development organizations which could offer a broad range of activities in support of small scale economic development as well as long-term planning for promotion, marketing, assistance, training and providing development and planning assistance to businesses and municipalities. I suppose it is an opportunity to recreate on a more local level the kind of activity the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency proposes to undertake on a regional level in Atlantic Canada.
Therefore, I would commend this particular amendment to the House. It improves upon Clause 7 and amplifies the ability of the Minister to create special areas under the Bill and have them defined in such a way as to provide these kinds of opportunities. It would make it clear that those opportunities
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
are available to integrate some of the activities of community development to bring about greater success and more opportunities in economic development initiatives.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question? The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus).

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few remarks on the motion submitted by my colleague. As someone who spent a number of years doing community development work in Thunder Bay, I can appreciate the need for this amendment to the Bill. As well, coming from an area that is similar in many ways to Atlantic Canada in terms of smaller populations, fewer centres and widely diverse communities, I recognize that we must be able to look at the smaller components. We must be able to allow locally based entrepreneurship of a co-operative nature to flourish. I think my colleague's amendment would help to facilitate that.
When we are talking about community based development projects, we are not talking about megaprojects. We are not talking about bringing in steel mills or automobile manufacturing facilities, we are talking about two, three, six, eight or 10 jobs being developed to provide a particular service or to meet a particular need in a community. Obviously, part of the goal is the creation of employment, but the other part of the goal is the furthering of the local economies to ensure that the people in these areas have the opportunities we have elsewhere in Canada.
I know that Atlantic Canada has a great history of community based development. In fact, there is a university in Atlantic Canada that is known throughout the world for its coop programs and its attitude toward teaching about the developing of co-operatives. I think it is ideal to enshrine this particular amendment in a Bill that deals with Atlantic Canada. It is appropriate to recognize that Atlantic Canada has as one of its key roots people working together against the elements and against an economy based outside their region to ensure that they too have opportunities.
Let me tell Hon. Members of an existing example of this in Atlantic Canada, the Kent-LEDA initiative. This is a federally funded local economic development agency with a total funding of $350,000. The Kent-LEDA organization has made debt and equity investments in numerous small projects and has provided counselling and technical assistance to local entrepreneurs.
The organization is directed by a group of local Kent area business people and invests, on average, in 10 new or expanding businesses a year. Thus far, its success rate compares favourably with DREE's former RDIA program. Ninety per cent of the firms in which it invested are still operating. It has created over 50 new jobs in a year in one of the most economically-depressed regions of the country.
There are also reasons to believe that this example gives a more accurate assessment of jobs created than those claimed

April 27, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
under DREE's old RDIA program. In many instances, LEDA represents the lender of last resort, so that the new businesses would not have gone ahead without its financing.
A community based organization that reviews proposals is composed of people who know the applicants. They know the track records of the applicants and they know how hard they are prepared to work. They also know their community. Rather than having a bureaucrat or a politician who is far removed either in a provincial capital or in the nation's capital have this opportunity, the local people will have the opportunity to help shape their own economy.
In my riding, the community of Atikokan has opted into the Community Futures Program. It has developed an excellent approach that will see not only community-based decisions made but it will see the tax dollars it has been given by the federal Government rolled over and over. As the business ventures it has invested in grow and it repays the loans, that money in turn will be invested back into the community once again. This is not an open-ended tap that will see tax dollars pour continuously into smaller areas, it is an investment.
We must recognize, as the motion states, that two communities in close proximity might have totally different economies. Yet they are lumped into the same catch-all category for Statistics Canada, for unemployment insurance and for the like. We should allow them to carve themselves out and to say that they are unique and should not be lumped in with community x or community y. This, I think, will be of great assistance to them. I would encourage Hon. Members to support my colleague's motion. I think it makes eminent sense.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak to this amendment because I think it is really important that it be adopted. One area where we have failed badly in this country concerns regional disparity. We have not taken into account the need to look at what local community development groups are all about. It seems to me some of the studies done on local economic development have recognized the fact that if we encourage co-ops and local groups to develop what they see as priorities in the local economy, not only are we making a sound investment but we are making it possible for long-term development to take place.
We have seen what mega projects from outside have done and it certainly has not been successful. What we are looking at here is the ability of an organization like the Community Futures Committee to be able to identify what its priorities are.
There have been some good examples right across the country where investments have been made in this type of community development, and they are still ongoing. Perhaps they are not as fancy as a huge factory which employs huge numbers of people, but they do not result in heavy lay-offs because of plant closures. Instead you find ongoing local community development.
It seems to me that it would have been a great advantage to a large part of the Canadian economy if we had done more work from the grass roots up rather than from the top down. Certainly this amendment will make that possible, and I commend my colleague for putting it forward. Certainly it will help the Atlantic region.
It is worth noting that more than 73,000 people in Newfoundland are involved in co-operatives. When we realize that, we recognize that this is an instrument we want to use in local community economic development.
As I said, I rose to speak on the amendment because I feel strongly that if we really do care about local economic development and people having some choice in where and how they are going to work, this amendment will make it possible.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this amendment. Many years ago I was an officer in the region of Inuvik in the Northwest Territories. In the process of trying to develop the kind of economic base necessary to keep certain communities going, it became very obvious that there was a need to designate areas in such a way that they could develop their own programs as part of the texture of the particular community rather than having something directed from the outside. To do this you must define your areas in very specific terms. You must also allow the kind of experimentation appropriate to that particular community.
Places like Newfoundland have seen a lot of attempts to impose development on them. In most cases large corporations come in and skim off the money allowed to them by provincial or federal Governments for development. They have no real vested interest in long-term job creation in those communities. Consequently, they have a tendency to take what they can as quickly as they can and leave. Instead of that, it is much more to the point to allow people who have a vested interest in the community to be part of the development. To do that, you have to direct the money very much more directly to those communities.
My colleague from St. John's mentioned Bell Island in northern Newfoundland. If someone goes in there once a week or once a month to try and direct development, it will not work particularly well. However, if you have assistance based in that community, it will work well. That is what is necessary to develop these kinds of programs so I call upon the House to support the amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the clauses in question are already extremely broad and give the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency the power to assist any enterprise in Atlantic Canada, including co-operative enterprises and the like. Therefore, I certainly do not see why we should support this amendment.
One has to wonder whether it is a deliberate tactic on the part of the NDP to have five, six or 10 speakers on each of these clauses in an attempt to hold up, for some reason, a Bill
April 27, 1988

which is so important to Atlantic Canada. We even had a contribution from the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) and former mayor of Ottawa. I would not be surprised if we get a contribution from her on every single blessed amendment.
One has to hope that the members of the NDP will be reasonable, short and pithy so we can vote on these amendments and send the Bill to the Senate where we will see what happens to it. The unelected Liberal majority there are coiled, ready to spring. I forecast that the Liberal majority in the Senate will not allow this legislation through. I believe the Celtic Sphinx is waiting there to pounce and that he has given orders to the Liberal caucus that they are not to let this Bill through the House. He vows that if it does go through the House, he will not let it through the Senate.
I trust NDP Members will assist us in getting it up to the Senate so we can test their mettle and see whether they are really going to prevent this kind of development in Atlantic Canada or not. Therefore, I ask Members to be reasonably pithy in their comments.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by reiterating what the Minister said regarding the length of time we spend on this. Bill C-103 was at second reading stage for 11 hours and four minutes, at which time 26 Members of the House took the opportunity to address it. The legislative committee spent 34 hours and 20 minutes on hearings and gave an opportunity for 73 witnesses to appear. Certainly there has been a fair amount of debate on this issue, and I share the concern that what we may be seeing today is an effort to drag this out and in some way deny the people of Atlantic Canada the benefits this legislation has to offer.
Speaking specifically to the amendment, the way the clause is worded now places only two restrictions on designated areas. One, they must be in Atlantic Canada. Two, they cannot extend to all of Atlantic Canada. In other words, designated areas, the way Clause 7 is currently written, could be within a province, could comprise the whole of a province, or even straddle two provinces. Therefore, this amendment is not necessary because the power already exists in Clause 7 to deal with a designated area.
The second amendment deals with a number of references to pilot projects in multi-year comprehensive area development strategies and so on. Clause 23 authorizes regulations to be made with respect to designated areas which vary from the generally applicable regulations. This will permit ACOA to give special treatment to areas which provide exceptional opportunities. With respect to pilot projects, strategies, action plans and so on, the agency, under its powers flowing from Clause 12, has been given the authority to undertake these types of initiatives.
Therefore, there is in this legislation adequate provision to cover both of the items outlined in the proposed amendments
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
and it is certainly not necessary for the House to accept the amendments proposed today.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a couple of words on the first amendment being proposed to this Bill which establishes ACOA, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. It should be renamed the "Atlantic Canada Overblown Agency" because there is nothing new in this legislation. The amendment introduced by the Hon. Member would, I suppose, ensure that the Minister has the power to carry out pilot projects and multi-year comprehensive area development strategies-whatever that means-and action plans and other means as necessary. All of this, of course, depends on the Minister. The clause says:
The Minister may, by order, establish as a designated area-where, in the
opinion of the Minister, exceptional circumstances-
What exceptional circumstances, Mr. Speaker? Could it be an election? Is that an exceptional circumstance? Could it be whether or not that particular area is represented by a government Member? Is that an exceptional circumstance?
As well, who is the Minister? According to the Bill the Minister is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary said: "Look at all the witnesses we had before the committee and all the Members who spoke before the committee". However, the person who introduced the Bill into the House of Commons did not appear before the committee, and that was the Prime Minister, the person who is moving the adoption of this particular Bill.
We all know that the Prime Minister is moving the adoption of the Bill because the Minister who has the authority under this Act is not here in this place at all. Where is he? I am not allowed to say where he is, am I? I am not even allowed to say where the Minister is. Someone listening to that would think it is a bit crazy that I am not allowed to say where he is. However, we are not allowed to say that. He is in what they call "the other place". In other words, he is not in this place here at all, not in the House of Commons. He is in the other place down the hall about a half a gunshot away. He is in the other place. He is not allowed to introduce something into this place, so the person who introduced it into this place is the Prime Minister who was not in his place to address the Bill in the first place. That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Motion No. 3.
That Bill C-103 be amended in Clause 12 by striking out line 28 at pages and substituting the following therefor:
"velopment of Atlantic Canada, and to reduce the economic disparity between Atlantic Canada and other regions of Canada, with particu-".
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is probably one of the most important motions before the House at report stage. The motion expounds upon the object, powers and duties of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency specified in Clause 12. The legislation written by the Government proposed that:
The object of the Agency is to support and promote opportunity for economic development of Atlantic Canada, with particular emphasis on small and medium-sized enterprises, through policy, program and project development and implementation and through advocacy of the the interests of Atlantic Canada in national economic policy, program and project development and implementation.
My motion indicates that one of the objects should also be "to reduce the economic disparity between Atlantic Canada and other regions of Canada". That is the core and the essence of what we in this Party think the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency ought to do. That is the pinnacle, the whole purpose of having this agency in the first place because of the astounding disparities that exist in the various regions of this country.
My Party and I make no apologies for the fact that in addition to myself, the Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar), to whom the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) referred as the former Mayor of Ottawa-and a fine mayor indeed she was-is speaking on this Bill. As the Mayor of Ottawa I would expect the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain to have great concern about regional disparity in this country. Members of this Party from other regions of Canada have already spoken on this Bill. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) from northern Ontario has spoken. He is interested in regional development, not only in northern Ontario where he and his constituents reside, but also in Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick. It is not only before those
Members of the House of Commons that we place this amendment. We place it before all Members of the House of Commons and in particular those Members who are not from the regions which suffer from the disparity that we have experienced in Newfoundland for many years.
I say shame to the Member for St. John's West for being upset that an Hon. Member from what we sometimes call Central Canada is concerned about issues of regional disparity. We need more Members like the Member for Hamilton Mountain to speak out in this House on issues of regional disparity and regional development. It is shameful for the Minister for International Trade to say that when someone does that there is something inherently wrong. It is a sign of the concern that this Party has for regional development that our Members from other parts of the country are willing to speak out on behalf of the needs of Newfoundlanders, Nova Scotians, New Brunswickers and Prince Edward Islanders who need the assistance of an agency such as the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency in order to reduce the disparities which exist.
Why is the Government afraid to put into the legislation a commitment to the reduction of regional disparity? It may or may not want to answer that question, but I have my own interpretation of the Government's action. It has developed an agency which does not have that goal. This is an agency that is basically designed to assist business and economic development. It has no goal to reduce the regional disparity between the Atlantic region and other regions of the country that are more prosperous. Without that objective, we simply see another agency to assist business and enhance the economy.
The amount of money the Government is allocating to this Agency is a measure of its commitment. If there was a real commitment toward the reduction of regional disparity, the Government would have committed substantially more funds to this Agency.
There is an increase of $200 million per year over a five-year period. This is the famous $1.05 billion we hear about. However, that money represents a five-year commitment for four provinces, amounting to $200 million a year.
The Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is close to $130 billion, $200 million of which, in addition to the other regular expenditures, is destined for the four provinces through this agency. That $200 million represents 15 per cent of 1 per cent of the entire Budget. It shows that the Government's priorities do not include the regional development that is required to reduce disparity.
The reduction of regional disparity is not a goal of this legislation because the Government has no real commitment toward reducing that disparity. Otherwise, it would be willing to be tested on its success in reducing regional disparity.

While there has been much discussion about government policy on regional disparity and regional development in the last 30 years, we have not seen any progress. Although the statistics I gave at second reading are quite startling, I will not repeat them again, except to say that some of those statistics show there has been very little progress and, in some cases no progress at all in the reduction of regional disparity between the Atlantic provinces and other regions of Canada.
This amendment is essential in order to focus the attention of the Agency, the Government, and the people of Canada on the elimination of regional disparity in this country. Regional disparity results in an inequality of opportunity not only for businesses, with which this legislation is concerned, but in areas like education, where there is a lack of opportunity and equality. That is what our Party aims to reduce.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the concept behind this amendment is not really new. It is certainly not the first time the Member has brought forward the topic of regional disparity and the impact the agency might have on that.
In the legislative committee an amendment was proposed by the Member that would provide in the five-year annual report from the Agency an evaluation of its activities and the impact of those activities upon regional disparity. However, to include it as it has been proposed by this amendment is really a negative concept of a Bill that I believe provides a very positive opportunity for Atlantic Canada.
This Bill promotes opportunities in Atlantic Canada. Certainly, as an Atlantic Canadian Member, I am much more anxious to promote opportunities than to go about measuring disparity. It has already been said that this Agency has a slender staff operation throughout Atlantic Canada and its efforts should focus on finding a way by which the Government of Canada, through Bill C-103, can help develop economic opportunities in that region of the country.
We are anxious to build upon what exists, and upon the opportunities that are presented in Atlantic Canada. This is more productive than making an effort to write a report and provide statistics that will really have no meaning. It would be extremely difficult to evaluate a reduction in disparity because one must be able to make the comparison. I presume the comparison would be between the Atlantic economy and the economy of another region, but is it northern Ontario, British Columbia, western Canada or central Canada? What does one measure it against? Certainly, the areas chosen for the comparison make a significant difference. I suggest, for instance, that there are parts of Atlantic Canada that are doing much better than other areas of Canada. If we measure that, we see great success in reducing disparity in Atlantic Canada.
On the other hand, there are other places which do not enjoy some of the benefits of the economic activity in central Canada and would not measure the same way. In that regard, it makes
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
very little sense to put verbiage in the legislation which does not have any real bearing in practical application.
It would also require us to make an evaluation when we do not have all the areas under our control. For example, the Atlantic economy could get very strong and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency could be expanding greatly those opportunities. As well, there could be an increase in the world price of oil and gas resulting in a resurgence of that industry in western Canada. Therefore, when we measure the western Canadian economy against eastern Canada, the results would really have nothing to do with the agency but with factors far beyond the control of the Minister and the legislation being put forward here today. If the economic activities on the Prairies declined as a result of a drought there, Heaven forbid, the disparity between those provinces and the Atlantic provinces would decrease. However, one cannot suggest that the Agency is very successful because another part of the country had the misfortune of a drought.
We want to put the staff time, energy and effort toward expanding our opportunities rather than measuring negative factors that really have no value in assessing how the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency works.
Obviously, we believe this amendment should be defeated because it is only verbiage that will not give us anything.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe this is a substantive and very important amendment. I suggest that if legislation is to lay out objectives, those objectives should be made very clear. The objectives listed in this Bill simply state that the Agency is designed to support and promote opportunities for the economic development of Atlantic Canada with particular emphasis on small and medium sized enterprises through policy program and project development and implementation, and through advocacy of the interests of Atlantic Canada in national economic policy program and project development and implementation.
It does not lay out its over-all objective, beyond a vague description of what it will be doing. It simply says that it will help. It does not lay out any reason for the help. It does not lay out any goal or any real objective which one would normally see stated in a statement of objectives in a new Bill for a new agency. My colleague from Newfoundland has proposed that that problem be corrected, that that shortcoming be rectified by giving it an objective, namely, to reduce the economic disparity between Atlantic Canada and other regions of Canada.
I do not think that we have to go out with very discreet measuring devices to know that Atlantic Canada has for quite a long time had a higher rate of unemployment than the rest of Canada. We do not have to do a lot of research or measuring to know that the incomes in Atlantic Canada are generally lower than in the rest of Canada. This sort of general knowledge has gone into some of the previous initiatives in the

April 27, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
country over the past 40 or 50 years. We have had forms of revenue sharing at the federal level with regard to tax revenues so that the lower income provinces have the benefit of increased revenues from the federal coffers. There has been quite a well established system for defining which are the have and which are the have-not provinces in this country.
It only makes sense if we are going to be proposing, as this Bill proposes to do, an economic development proposal for a particular region in the country that one of the clear mandates of that new agency should be to try to reduce the economic disparity that now exists and is recognized with or without any further measuring techniques. It is there and measured each year when the amount of funding to go to revenue sharing is decided upon. This work is already being done. It is simply a test that one would give oneself as a manager or a Minister in charge of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, to see whether or not some ground is being gained or not.
I think that if the Minister, whoever it is, goes into his or her job without having any objective other than to interfere in Atlantic Canada, no further vision as to what the role of government should be in Atlantic Canada, that Atlantic Canadians will not gain anything from this particular initiative.
We do not think that this handcuffs the Minister in any way. It provides him and future Ministers with a very laudable goal, one of decreasing the economic disparity that now exists and is measured and is known for Atlantic Canadians. We think it is a very useful item to be put into the Bill as one of the main objectives of this legislation.
It is something that this and future Ministers can use as their target to say: "If I am Minister of this Agency my job is to reduce the economic disparity between the Atlantic region and the rest of Canada. I will therefore attempt to reduce unemployment and to increase incomes on investment in this particular area". This is something that the Bill does not now give as a mandate for the Minister. I think this amendment would correct that shortfall.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Harris (St. John's East) moved:
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-103 be amended in Clause 12 by adding immediately after line
35 at page 4 the following:
"(2) In carrying out its object the Agency shall ensure that there be equity between the Atlantic Provinces in the allocation of resources, effort and programs in a manner to be determined by the Agency, and the Agency shall report annually to Parliament on the fulfillment of this objective.
He said: Motion No. 4 provides a direction to the Agency that in carrying out its object-this is right after the objects clause that we just discussed-it shall ensure that there be equity between the Atlantic provinces in the allocation of resources, effort and programs in a manner to be determined by the Agency, and the Agency shall report annually to Parliament on the fulfilment of this objective.
I suppose it speaks for itself in terms of what we are aiming at with respect to this amendment. The reason that this is necessary is that because this particular Agency as devised by the Government is one that is designed to be responsive to applications generated in particular by business enterprises.
We know that as a part of the disparity between the Atlantic region and other parts of Canada that there are disparities in the level of development of business enterprise, the level of development of entrepreneurial enterprises, from one region to the other.
Within the Atlantic region there is a similar type of disparity. In some areas of the Atlantic region there are large numbers of corporations that are active in enterprise and ready to put in their applications and take advantage of any program that might be devised. We have seen that not only in the Atlantic region, but in the operations of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which was a predecessor of DRIE. The consequences are that these programs that were originally set up to support regional development ended up helping regional development in north Toronto, and regional development programs ended up responding to requests, demands, and lobbying from larger business enterprises.
In the first period since the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency was announced on June 6, 1987 in St. John's, Newfoundland, we have seen the expenditure of this Agency operate in accordance with that type of history. We have seen the programs administered by that Agency respond again to
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
the same types of economic forces where there was a certain level of development; in some cases development already promoted by government as in the case of Cape Breton, and in other cases driven by other aspects of the economy, as in the case of other parts of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. I am told that there are some dozens of times more in absolute quantity of business enterprises in New Brunswick than there are in the Province of Newfoundland.
From June 6 to February 29 under programs such as the Atlantic Enterprise Program and the IRDP program, which when one includes loan insurance as well as the IRDP, the Atlantic Enterprise, and the IBD contributions, the expenditures total $126 million. Of that money, $63 million was spent in Cape Breton alone, which is part of one province. In Newfoundland $9.4 million was spent in the whole province with a population in the range of five times more than that of Cape Breton. In Nova Scotia, exclusive of Cape Breton Island, there was an expenditure of $19 million. In Prince Edward Island $5.3 million was spent out of a total $126 million. In New Brunswick $20 million was spent.
Therefore, we have a concern that in carrying out its programs the Agency itself, which is supposed to promote the economic development of the Atlantic region, will be favouring one region or one province, or one part of a province over another. That is not necessarily by design, but merely by something akin to the law of the jungle.
If a business enterprise, or a large number of business enterprises in the Province of Nova Scotia are ready because they have sufficient equity or have in place their business plan or market plan and have the backing and the financing for a percentage of a project and know that they can get the rest of it from ACOA, then they will be off and running. Whereas, in some parts of Atlantic Canada, and I am particularly concerned about Newfoundland, the enterprises and the entrepreneurs with the ideas and the projects, the activities and the plans, while being very good plans that would promote and lead to economic development in their region, will be left behind. Perhaps they will be smaller and not be able to take the same advantage of programs that may be offered to the whole Atlantic region.
This amendment would force the Agency to ensure that if the programs that it already had, or had been handed over from other Departments, or those it devised on its own, were acting in a way that was not fair to all of the provinces, that others would be devised which perhaps would have a particular application to the Province of Newfoundland, or the Province of Prince Edward Island, or in some other way would balance the equity between the provinces with respect to this program.
I think that there are ways of doing that. There are ways of allocating resources that are equitable. They are not included in the proposed amendment. They are available for the Agency to design and to decide those measures and formulas, if formulas are needed, but the requirement, in addition to ensuring equity between the provinces, is that they must report

April 27, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
annually on how they achieve equity. The Agency must say that it has a certain set of standards, "Here is how we applied them and here is how we achieved equity". If we do not like that, we can argue about it in the House and propose other amendments. But we will know what the Agency is doing and what the justification is. If we leave it to the Agency's own devices, we do not know what will happen, and after the fact we will be wondering what went on and be attempting to get some justification from the Government on it.
It is a big concern because we do not want to see Newfoundland fighting with Cape Breton or Prince Edward Island fighting with New Brunswick over the allocation of money for a program that is supposed to benefit the entire region. I have a fear that that might happen, if the Agency is not told from the very beginning to pay attention to this principle and ensure equity between all four provinces. The Agency is to report annually on what progress has been made, or if the programs were lopsided one year, then what it plans to do the next year to make up the balance. I do not think it is a very long way to go to insist that an agency of the Government be fair as between the provinces in the operation of this particular program.
The Atlantic provinces are not a homogeneous unit. There are problems of development that are different in Newfoundland than those in Nova Scotia. This fear is not merely my own. It was expressed by the Newfoundland Government in its discussion paper presented to the Government in December, 1986. It proposed a formula of allocation based on some type of regional disparity index that it devised. It looked at such issues as low earned income and the unemployment rate. The gross provincial product, the low earned income per capita, and the unemployment rate are three factors that could influence a disparity indicator which would show that a particular province deserves more attention than perhaps another province in terms of handing out the funds.
I am not suggesting any rigid formula to the Agency. I am suggesting that the Agency adopt, and be forced to adopt by legislation, the principle of equity between the provinces, and report to Parliament annually on how it has achieved that in order that we could determine in committee, or wherever, whether the Agency has applied the funds fairly.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak for a moment on this particular clause. It is a very straightforward and direct requirement to recognize that there are diverse provinces and regions that in some cases, have different requirements and different amounts of regional disparity. This particular clause does not establish a basis on which the Government or the Agency must deal with these differentials and disparities, but it recognizes that it is the Agency's responsibility to look at each of the provinces and ensure equity between those provinces and regions as they are defined in the Act.
Mr. Walpole, in giving a definition of what he considered to be economic disparity, suggested that regional disparity existed where the earned income of a particular area was no more than two-thirds of the Canadian average. In establishing equity as between the various regions of Atlantic Canada, one might look at that standard of disparity, with the attempt being to bring the Atlantic provinces as close as possible to the Canadian average.
That is the kind of equity which Clause 12 would require of the Agency.
To my mind, it is fairly straightforward, and it is a point on which the Agency should be given direction.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read, with interest, the proposed amendment. As well, I have listened to the various comments made thus far in the debate. Those promoting the amendment constantly refer to how flexible it would be, and the fact that it would not be necessary to do certain things.
Let me read the proposed amendment:
In carrying out its object the agency shall ensure that there be equity
between the Atlantic Provinces-
The use of the word "shall" implies that there be some kind of a formula by which the Agency "shall" ensure that there be equity between the Atlantic provinces.
The amendment goes on to talk about equity "in the allocation of resources".
Like the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) I, too, have some statistics in respect of the ACOA program from June 6, 1987 to March 31, 1988. I could read you some of these numbers and ask you to tell me what is equitable. For example, it talks about the authorized contributions in the Province of New Brunswick under IRDP and the AEP being SI5 million. In Nova Scotia it was $31 million.
Does that constitute equity? In the Province of Newfoundland, it was $9 million. But when one looks at that in conjunction with the loan insurance, the numbers change considerably, with Newfoundland moving up to $44 million; Nova Scotia to $81 million; and New Brunswick, to $63 million. Is that equity?
When one looks at the special category of Cape Breton, no reference is made to it. I presume from the lack of a reference that it is included in the figures for the Province of Nova Scotia. When one looks at the programs in the context of the federal moneys they have been able to deliver to Cape Breton, one sees that the contribution is $50 million, and that the authorized loan insurance is $17 million.
There is nothing in the proposed amendment that would separate Cape Breton from Nova Scotia. In that circumstance, how does one measure that? If there are special programs for Cape Breton-something which will be discussed later in this
April 27, 1988

debate-should we then ensure that that much more goes into New Brunswick, into Prince Edward Island, and into Newfoundland?
We are all aware of the difficulties that have been experienced in attracting industry to Cape Breton. Is that equity?
We can talk about equity in terms of the number of jobs created. In Newfoundland, for a total projected cost of $44 million, 692 jobs were created. But in Nova Scotia, for a projected cost of $81 million, only 520 jobs were created; and for New Brunswick, at $63 million, 583 jobs. How does one measure equity in the allocation of resources?
The amendment then goes on to speak of "equity of effort". That is a dandy! I would like to be able to measure "equity of effort". I do not know precisely what one would measure. There are offices in Newfoundland, in New Brunswick, in Prince Edward Island, in Cape Breton, and in Nova Scotia. Who is going to run around measuring the "effort" of the employees of those various offices in terms of the delivery of this program?
Motion No. 12, to be debated later, talks about the assignment of existing employees.
I can envisage a real scramble around the managerial table to ensure that they do not get anyone who will not be able to add to the "effort" of that particular office, because someone, somehow, is going to run around and measure that effort.
The last item in the trilogy relates to the measuring of the "equity of programs".
One of the aims of this legislation is that the Minister, in conjunction with his advisory board, have the opportunity to create programs, to designate areas. But all of a sudden, he must ensure that there is equity as between the provinces. That, in my view, would seriously limit the flexibility that the Minister must have.
The amendment also talks about the Agency reporting annually to Parliament in respect of the fulfilment of the objective of equity. One can immediately envisage the scurry in New Brunswick to rush an application through on December 31 in order to have that reflected in the annual report on the equity of resources.
I would much prefer that the Agency take its time and make its decisions on applications on their merit. The criterion should not be merely to justify a bureaucrat's annual report in respect of equity in the allocation of resources.
To my mind, this amendment, among others, would bring about a situation in Atlantic Canada which was not contemplated by the legislation itself. Certainly, it would decrease the flexibility of the Agency. The Atlantic Canada Opportunities Program is not meant to be an entitlement program. We just got rid of an entitlement program in the context of the various tiers in past programs. As a representative of a municipality on
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
the edge of another tier, I can tell you that I have seen industry move just across the border in order to get additional benefits.
We do not want to entitle a certain region or a certain province to a given amount of money under this program; rather, we want all Atlantic Canadians to have the opportunity to chase after every economic opportunity that presents itself.
In reading the proposed amendment, the implication is that moneys will have to be withheld from certain areas in order to achieve equity as between the provinces. What about putting more money into given areas? If there is a bona fide economic opportunity in Newfoundland, I want to ensure that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be able to provide funding and assistance to that area in order that the economic benefit can be achieved.
The Agency has to be able to take advantage of every opportunity presented. I do not want the Agency placed in the position of having to deny an application on the basis that to approve it would be to throw out of whack the "equity" formula.
If this amendment is adopted, a formula will have to be devised in order to ensure that there is equity in the allocation of resources, effort and programs as between the Atlantic provinces.
To my mind, the best way to ensure fair and equitable allocation of the resources of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency within Atlantic Canada is to rely upon the parliamentary process, with the parliamentary representatives of these areas making the appropriate representations to the Minister, to the employees of the Agency. In that way, there will be every opportunity for good projects to get positive consideration. It should not be done in accordance with some formula, or in accordance with some numbers set by Ottawa in respect of achieving equity between the Atlantic provinces in the allocation of resources.
As a Member of Parliament from Atlantic Canada, I would not want to run up against any such formula. I want to be in a position to fight as hard as I can for any project that is going to be good for my region of the Province of New Brunswick; and as an Atlantic Canadian Member of Parliament, I will fight hard to ensure that every economic opportunity that presents itself in Atlantic Canada gets every consideration possible from the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
For all of the reasons I have set out, I do not think we should consider accepting this amendment. Any amendment that would result in someone going around measuring equity of resources, equity of effort, or equity of programs should be rejected.

speechtext:
Motion No. 6.
That Bill C-103 be amended in Clause 13 by striking out line 37 at page 4 and substituting the following therefor:
"shall".
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the clause in which the Government spells out exactly what the Agency is responsible for. Clause 13 starts out by saying, "In carrying out its object," and we already dealt with the object of the Agency. In carrying out this object for economic development, which is
April 27, 1988

very all-encompassing and broad, "the Agency," and then it spells out for two or three pages what the Agency's intentions are.
The Bill provides, for example, that the Agency will support business associations, it will study the development of business opportunities, it will improve business communications, it will promote scholarship related to business, it will assist investors, it will make loans to people, it will guarantee repayments and it will do practically everything. However, it will do nothing because the key word in Clause 13 is "may". The Bill says that in carrying out its object which is contained in the previous clause, the Agency may do this and the Government may do that.
The purpose of this amendment is to say that the Agency shall do these things. There is quite a difference between the words "may" and "shall". "May", according to the Oxford English Dictionary, means expressing possibility. That is not what we are dealing with here today. These hundreds of people will be paid such great salaries to belong to an agency in Atlantic Canada. We want to make sure they do something, not just express the possibility of doing something. Therefore, I suggest we substitute the word "shall" for the word "may". The word "shall" according to the dictionary means that it is a command, or an obligation to do what the Act says it will do. What is the sense in having an Act if the agency you are creating need not do anything in the Act? That is precisely what this particular clause is all about.
We spoke a few moments ago about equality. There is no equality under this Agency when you have, for example, 17 employees in Newfoundland, 14 in Prince Edward Island, and far more in Ottawa, as is presently the case.
This amendment is very clear. It simply changes the word "may" to "shall" and forces the Agency, as the Bill suggests, in concert with concerned departments and agencies of all Governments in Atlantic Canada, to carry out its responsibilities. It will have no choice, it has to carry out its responsibilities or it should not be in existence. That is the purpose of the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, when we apply what the Hon. Member is saying to a few parts of this particular clause it may not look too bad. However, I am going to show you some parts of the Bill where it will certainly make a difference when you apply the program to Atlantic Canada.
One of the things that is so important in this legislation is that the Agency have as much flexibility as possible so that it can choose the appropriate program instrument according to the circumstances. The Agency can look at an application from Prince Edward Island and decide which program will give the most beneficial kind of support to the application. Obviously we are concerned about flexibility, and normally in legislative drafting program authority is discretionary. The Minister can determine the allocation of resources in the most appropriate
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
manner possible in order to take advantage of the biggest number of economic opportunities in Atlantic Canada.
Having said that, if you change the word "may" on page 4 to "shall" it would probably not be a big concern with regard to Clause 13(a), (b) or (c), but when you get down to Clause 13(d) it will say:
-shall
(d)	assist investors-
What if they do not want assistance? What if they do not want, unfortunately, to establish an enterprise in Atlantic Canada? We shall assist them whether they want assistance or not. Going on a little further to Clause 13(e):
-shall
(e)	make loans to any person with respect to the establishment and
development of enterprises-
What if they decide that this is not the proper procedure and the guy does not want a loan? Perhaps he wants something under IRDP or ERDA. No, we shall make a loan. You do not know what is good for you and we are going to give you a loan. He might prefer a direct contribution with nothing to be repaid. The circumstances in the particular area where the application is generated may dictate that that instrument be applied, but according to this amendment we are going to give him a loan. Then it goes on to say:
-shall
(f)	guarantee the repayment-
What if we do not want it back? What if it is a direct contribution from one of the programs? No, we shall guarantee repayment. Or, we shall guarantee loan insurance or credit insurance. What if they do not need it? According to this amendment we shall go out and make sure they get loan insurance or credit insurance.
The amendment may look all right when you talk about planning or directing and managing and so on, but one of the key elements of this legislation, and I do not know how they missed this in the 11 hours of debate on second reading and 34 hours in committee, is to provide flexibility so that we can provide the optimum federal government assistance in a particular area of the Atlantic provinces so that we can all expand our economic opportunities. We want that flexibility, and adoption of this amendment will not allow us that flexibility. It will not allow the applicants the flexibility we now have with the current wording.
