He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion was suggested by many Members of Parliament from Atlantic Canada and people who appeared before the standing committee who are concerned that nowhere in the Bill is it mentioned that the fishery, agriculture, and mining would qualify for programs under the Agency being established by the Government of Canada.
There is nothing at all wrong with this amendment. You will note that various parts of the clause to be amended emphasize "particularly" this or that. What is wrong with inserting "with emphasis on the utilization of primary resources, particularly the fishery and agriculture in Atlantic Canada"? There is nothing wrong with putting particular emphasis on the primary resources of Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island which remain underutilized and underdeveloped. We know that the fishery is underdeveloped and underutilized. The Government of Canada and the provincial Governments in Atlantic Canada, particularly the Government of Newfoundland, will have to pay special attention to the utilization of primary resources, particularly in the fishery, to create finished products. There should be particular emphasis as well on agriculture in Atlantic Canada.
It was brought up in this House one day that the potatoes which are used on government jets and by Air Canada and VIA Rail are actually imported from Belgium. If you board a VIA Rail train in Moncton, New Brunswick, where the Parliamentary Secretary is from, you are served potatoes which were grown in Belgium. That is not very nice. If you board an Air Canada jet at an international airport in Atlantic
Government Organization Act. Atlantic Canada, 1987
Canada the potatoes you are served are from Belgium and the cake is from Holland.
Through this motion we want particular emphasis put on our primary resources; our fishing industry, our agricultural industry, and our mining industry in Atlantic Canada under this Agency. Why not spell it out? They spell out data banks and networks and investment requirements in various industries. Why not spell out the industries which are important to Atlantic Canada?
There is no reason in the world why the Government cannot accept this amendment. In fact, by not accepting the amendment the Government is saying that it does not agree that the primary resources; the fishery, agriculture, and mining, are the most important aspects of economic development in Atlantic Canada. In other words, the Government does not know anything about economic opportunities in Atlantic Canada.
The problem in Atlantic Canada is that the money has not been directed to the area to which it should be directed, that is, to making finished products with our primary resources rather than exporting them to foreign countries and then buying them back. We are exporting the jobs in our fishing industry to the eastern United States. Frozen cod blocks are thawed out in Massachusetts where thousands of people are employed. Companies like National Sea Products and Fishery Products International, which are being supported all the time by the Government of Canada, are making loads of money.
It should be spelled out in the Bill that it pays particular attention to the mining resources of Cape Breton Island, the fishery in Cape Breton Island and agriculture in Cape Breton Island, just as it does throughout the Atlantic provinces.
The Government will not accept this amendment because it is afraid to do so. It does not want to get involved in the primary industries of Atlantic Canada, or to create jobs in Atlantic Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on the amendment. While the amendment looks very nice, I am sure it is playing to a certain audience, nonetheless its contents are covered in the legislation and in the wording currently proposed.
The philosophy behind Bill C-103 is to provide support where opportunities exist in Atlantic Canada for economic development. The agency has the flexibility to respond to all opportunities to get involved in good business proposals. Emphasizing one or two sectors in Atlantic Canada would only serve to unbalance the approach that is being adopted in Bill C-103.
Where in the agriculture and the fisheries industry there are opportunities, ACOA will have a role to play. If there is an opportunity and a business is involved in agriculture, in fishing, in forestry or in mining, then ACOA is anxious to assist them in the development of that opportunity.
In addition to that, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) currently have programs to assist people in those sectors. Provinces have programs, as does the federal Government through those two Departments. Obviously, ACOA does not necessarily want to parallel those programs and to provide an overlap. It wants to fill its role in order to co-ordinate the effort of Governments toward those various sectors.
April 27, 1988

When we look at the legislation we see that it is clear in this clause that it will help in the promotion of enterprises, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, and when they are available in those sectors ACOA will have a role to play and will be glad to provide assistance. However, when we look at other clauses in the legislation, for example, Clause 5, we see that it deals with the fact that the Minister may exercise powers and perform duties and functions that affect economic opportunity and development in Atlantic Canada over which Parliament has jurisdiction and that are not by or pursuant to law assigned to any other Member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, or to any Department, board or agency of the Government. So if there is an opportunity in a sector that is not assigned to someone else, then there is an opportunity for ACOA to get involved.
Clause 9 deals with a rather unique aspect of the legislation. It states:
Where the Minister is satisfied that the implementation of a program or project authorized by any other Act would further the purpose of this Part, the Minister may, conditionally or unconditionally, undertake to transfer funds appropriated for the purposes of this Part to supplement funds that the Minister responsible for the program or project has undertaken to expend in connection therewith.
In other words, if there is an opportunity in the agriculture industry, the forestry sector or the mining sector and there is not enough money in an existing program, then the Minister can say: "We are going to put Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency money into that program to supplement funds of the national program or programs that are available in the other Department".
There is a great deal of flexibility here. The Hon. Member mentioned the fisheries industry. Just yesterday there was an announcement with respect to a company called Pioneer Fisheries which is involved in a lobster holding and marketing plant on Prince Edward Island. It has received a $1.3 million grant to begin operation. This is an example of a business opportunity in the fisheries sector in which the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency has responded.
It can happen. It is happening. These amendments are not necessary for it to happen. Obviously, we feel that the measures are provided for in the legislation as it exists. The operation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency interprets it that way. This is a good example of assistance being provided to one of those primary sectors to which this amendment makes reference.
We feel the matter is adequately covered in Bill C-103 as it exists. There is absolutely no need for the adoption of this amendment.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Motion No. 9
That Bill C-103 be amended in Clause 18 by striking out line 29 at page 7
and substituting the following therefor:
"each province in Atlantic Canada and shall be broadly representative of
the business, social cultural, governmental and educational participants in the
economic development of Atlantic Canada."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this particular motion proposes to amend Clause 18 which provides for the establishment of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Board consisting of the President and not more than 18 other members appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister.
This motion will amend Clause 18(3) which presently states, "The Board shall include persons from each province in Atlantic Canada", to state, "The Board shall include persons from each province in Atlantic Canada and shall be broadly representative of the business, social, cultural, governmental and educational participants in the economic development of Atlantic Canada".
The reason for that amendment is to attempt to ensure that the Board giving advice which is required to assist the Agency in carrying out its functions shall not only have representatives such as those it presently has. The Minister has appointed 18 people in addition to the President, most of whom are business people. There are representatives from three Governments and one agency, and there is one person who is involved with the labour movement. But in its composition the Board does not have anyone from the academic community assigned, or people who are involved in the type of economic development organizations that I have mentioned.

April 27, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
There is no one from the co-operative sector. When this was raised at second reading, the Agency went out of its way to announce that co-operatives were included. But it was not very clear from the attitude of the Government, particularly in terms of the make-up of the Board, that this was the case. In fact, people are phoning me from New Brunswick and Newfoundland and saying that ACOA does not know how to deal with co-operatives, and that they are not even sure that ACOA understands what a co-operative is. I was informed that someone in New Brunswick was told not to set up a cooperative because that will take a long time to get organized; do it through a business corporation. This was a co-operative that wanted to set up a co-operative enterprise. The Agency was either ignorant or insensitive to that type of development or economic enterprise.
The Agency might state in its brochure or in its policy that it provides assistance to co-operatives, but if it does not know what co-operatives are or how they act, or has no experience with the history of co-operatives in the Maritime provinces and in Newfoundland and the important role that they play in economic development, how can programs be devised and economic development assisted with those types of agencies?
Today the Speaker ruled out of order a motion to set up an advisory committee. To remind the House, the motion states:
(4) The Minister shall establish an advisory board comprised of women to advise on the policies and programs necessary to ensure that women participate in the activities and initiatives of the Agency, and provide for the membership and further duties and functions of such a board.
That motion was ruled out of order. But in this particular motion there could be provision to include representatives of women's organizations to insist that the Agency, in operating its programs and in devising its staffing and other activities, pay special attention to the needs of women in business. Because they have different approaches, they have different needs in order to move forward and develop economic programs and business enterprises.
This particular amendment will provide diversity and broad representation needed to make the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency aware of what is going on in Atlantic Canada, aware of the role played by co-operatives, by women in business, by the community economic development corporations, by the regional development associations, by the academic community that has concerns and ideas, and by the scientific community.
With this amendment we are asking that the Board be required to be broadly representative of those parts of society that are furthering economic development, and not only business people. Business people have a very important role to play in economic development. That is important, and perhaps even primarily important in terms of the make-up of a particular board. We do want people with business experience, and people with successful business experience who are aware of what it takes to make a successful project work.
We also want the Agency to understand the broad range of economic development activity that takes place in the Atlantic region, in the fishery, in the mining industry, and in the regional development sector that has been very active in Newfoundland and also in other provinces over the last number of years. They have a very important role to play. They have an understanding of communities in Atlantic Canada that perhaps some of the more successful businessmen might not have, if they are operating in larger centres. We want to see more of a balance than we have received. Without having the Minister told that the Board has to be broadly representative, we would like to see more of a variety in the appointments. We think that this amendment would achieve that end, and I would ask the House to support it fully.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, a word of support for this amendment. For the life of me, I cannot see why the Government would not agree to the amendment. As it is presently worded, Clause 18(3) states, "The Board shall include persons from each province in Atlantic Canada". It says "persons", Mr. Speaker. I suppose there could be one from one province, three from another province, and five from yet another province. They could all be defeated Progressive Conservative candidates. They could be defeated politicians. The amendment asks for the Board to be representative of the business community, social and cultural agencies. In other words, representative of the people in Atlantic Canada.
I would like to see a couple of people on the Board who are unemployed, or a couple of people on the Board who are used to drawing unemployment insurance, or a couple of people on the Board who tried setting up businesses in Atlantic Canada but went broke. Perhaps the Board could include a couple of community leaders from town councils who were elected by the people in those smaller communities in Atlantic Canada. In fact, probably it should be spelled out even more than it presently is. The Minister is the person who will appoint the Board, and you know, Mr. Speaker, who those people would be if the present Minister appointed them. I do not mean the Minister who introduced the Bill, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), but the Minister who is in the other place who is responsible for this particular legislation.
I cannot see why the Government would not accept the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment presented by the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris). Coming from the Yukon, as I do, the opposite end of the country to Atlantic Canada, I can very much relate to the need to have such an advisory board. I would draw an analogy between the capacity of this Board and the care with which members of the Board should be selected so as to represent a broad range of interests, including that of the business community.
April 27, 1988

I note that the Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses, the small business association, has expressed the concern that this Board will not represent the interests of small business; that, rather, it will only represent the interests of the large business sector.
That is an extremely important point. As has also been mentioned, women's interests should also be represented on this Board. Women constitute an ever-increasing proportion of the entrepreneurs in our society. Between 1972 and 1983, the number of women entrepreneurs increased by some 140 per cent, while the number of male entrepreneurs increased by only 10 per cent.
In light of those figures, the interests of women present a significant emerging factor in terms of representation on such a Board.
Knowing the Atlantic region as I do, the question of rural and urban representation is an extremely important one. The opportunities available to non-urban areas are often more difficult to create, given the smaller population available to a business, with the result that non-urban areas are often overlooked. I think it extremely important that any such advisory board reflect the rural/urban split as well.
I realize that no advisory board can represent all interests, and indeed it should not be merely a collection of separate interests. However, we have seen all too often that such advisory boards are somewhat uni-dimensional, lacking in representation from the less vocal segments of our society, thereby making it more difficult for those segments to develop activities which will enhance their economic development.
The Department of Employment and Immigration has established local advisory committees whose purpose it is to advise on how projects and programs under that Department are to be allocated. One can easily draw a parallel between that and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Under both, there is an attempt to reflect, in the projects undertaken, the different sectors of society, the large/small business community, and the rural/urban split.
In summary, I strongly support the proposed amendment. Through this amendment, the various sectors of the community can have adequate representation on the advisory board, thus enabling them to take maximum advantage of the programs offered.

He said: Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 11 asks and requires the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency in its annual report to make a statement on the annual impact of its operations on regional disparity between Atlantic Canada and other regions of Canada. I am speaking as a Newfoundlander and as an Atlantic Canadian.
I resent the implication from the government side of the House, the Deputy House Leader, that nobody else in this

April 27, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
House has the right to speak on regional disparity and to speak up for people in other parts of the country. If that is the standard by which the Government will judge the actions of people on this side of the House when they are speaking for the rights of Canadians, I think it is time the Government was thrown out and tossed to the wolves where it belongs.
To hear the very Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) come to this House and speak up in support of legislation that is good for Atlantic Canada, that is what we expect in Atlantic Canada. If she did not, I would condemn her for it. If she refused to support Atlantic Canada, I would condemn her as I would condemn the Government House Leader saying that by doing that she is somehow pretending to be interested in the people of Canada. It is this side of the House, particularly our Party, which is fighting hard for legislation and fighting to improve this legislation so that Atlantic Canadians are protected. I welcome any addition to the debate which the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain can make.
I would encourage other Members from the central Canadian cities and towns, from the areas of Canada which are doing very well by this economy, to stand up and support legislation and support improvements to legislation that will protect Atlantic Canada. That is what is wrong with this whole issue. There are not enough people who are not from Atlantic Canada who have stood up for Atlantic Canada. If we had more people in this House who represent the richer parts of the country, the parts that are doing better than Atlantic Canada, speaking and being concerned about all of Canada, then we would not be dealing here today with a Bill designed to try to make up for what has been lost by neglect and the fact that Atlantic Canada has been denied its rightful place in Confederation. I think the comments of the Hon. Deputy House Leader, the Minister of State (Mr. Lewis), underline and underscore the real problem in Atlantic Canada.
In Newfoundland we have seven Members. Some of us are louder than others. We hear from the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) quite often. I try to speak out as often as I can and as loud as I can, sometimes louder than others, but there are only seven of us in this large House.
In Atlantic Canada, there are not enough people to form a majority to vote in anything that the rest of the country does not want. We are divided up into Parties as well. We expect and rely upon the support of Members from other parts of Canada within our own Party and, hopefully, even within other Parties, to support Atlantic Canada when measures are being brought forth that are for the benefit of Atlantic Canada.
This particular measure emphasizes the need for this Agency to report annually and to focus on regional disparities and the indicators that are present. I will give one example of what is going on in Atlantic Canada. One economic indicator which is a most valuable one to test regional development and
the economic support in the economy is that of earned income per capita. Earned income per capita is income that does not come from social assistance or unemployment insurance but from earnings. Earned income per capita is a very good measure of the economic health of a region.
At the time of confederation in 1949, the ratio of earned income per capita in Newfoundland compared to that of all of Canada, the Canadian average, was 48.8 per cent. The average earned income per capita in Newfoundland was 48.8 per cent of the national average. Do you know what it is now, Mr. Speaker? I bet you do not. After 38 years of confederation, it is now 55.5 per cent of the Canadian average. That is the progress we have made in 38 years. We are now 6 per cent closer to the national average in earned income per capita.
At that rate, do you know how long it will take us to reach the national average, Mr. Speaker? It will take 288 years. That is how long we will have to wait, yet when the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain rises to speak out in favour of Atlantic Canada, she is accused of pretending to be interested.
After the next election, I hope we will have many, many more Members here like the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain, Members who no matter what part of the country they are elected from, whether from the Prairies, northern Ontario, central Ontario, southern Ontario or British Columbia, will support regional development measures in Atlantic Canada, a commitment to not having to wait 288 years for the kind of progress that is needed but to demanding and insisting that there be equality now. We must work quickly to reduce the regional disparities in Canada and to ensure that there is equality of opportunity across the country.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment deals with the staffing of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and with the public servants, particularly in the Department of DRIE. During the course of the establishment of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, many of them were given notice or were told that they were to be made redundant as a result of the creation of this agency.
While the legislative committee was in Charlottetown, the Professional Institute of Public Servants wrote a letter advising the Minister from the other place and made a presentation to the committee in Charlottetown advising us that long-term professional public servants who were quite capable of operating in various parts of the Public Service were being denied an opportunity to work at the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. This was a very different approach from that which was taken in the establishment of the Western Diversification Office.
The Minister responsible for that Agency assured all those working in DRIE or at the other Agencies or programs that were being transferred to the Western Diversification Program that they would have an opportunity to work in that Agency and that there would be no redundancies as a result of that move. There were sufficient person-years in the complement of the new Agency to accommodate all of those who would be affected by changes in the transferring of the program.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The Senator from the other place who was responsible for this legislation made no such commitment to the public servants of Atlantic Canada. A large number of them are being made redundant and there is no reason for that. There are plenty of person-years available and perhaps 100 person-years more than necessary in the new Agency to cover these people. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary will probably have the exact figures at hand. It is quite clear that there is sufficient person-years in the new Agency to take care of all those who were working on programs that had been transferred to the Agency.
If these public servants were quite capable and professional and were working in other Departments properly implementing programs that have now been transferred, why are they no longer acceptable to the Public Service? Why is it that they are not being treated in the same manner as their western counterparts were? If these public servants were incapable of carrying out their duties, they should have been fired when they were working at their previous jobs. They should have been disciplined or there should have been some procedure to deal with them. They should not simply be made redundant so that the Government can hire 300 or 400 more people rather than ensuring that these public servants are transferred and given first choice at jobs available in the new Agency. This amendment would ensure that those public servants are treated fairly.

They are good people and will probably have in most cases an opportunity to go over to ACOA.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just by way of explanation, when the legislation was drafted it made reference only to Cape Breton. Some of the provisions of the legislation applied to an area just on the edge of the Strait of Canso in addition to Cape Breton Island. The Government looks upon the whole area around the Canso Causeway on both sides of the strait as an economic unit for purposes of the Cape Breton tax credit. The committee had an opportunity to visit that area and we saw that Port Hawkesbury on one side and Mulgrave on the other were co-operating with regard to industrial development around the causeway and on both sides of the Strait of Canso.
When it came to the attention of the Government that the definition in this Bill did not include the part across the Canso Strait it was agreed that we would add it. We had considerable debate in committee and a little posturing and, I am sure, game playing and it was unfortunately not unanimously agreed to. The Royal Recommendation is to add that part of the Cape Breton tax credit area to the legislation as it relates to ACOA and the enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to Motion No. 15 which was ruled out of order, as was Motion No. 14, the one we are now discussing. The motion would add the Town of Mulgrave to the definition of Cape Breton Island. That town is not on Cape Breton Island, as I am sure you are well aware. I am sure that the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) is well aware of that. Indeed, I am sure all the people on Cape Breton are well aware that Mulgrave is not on Cape Breton Island. It is on the other side of the strait. There are a number of other little towns along the Canso Strait going down to the Town of Canso which are also not on Cape Breton Island.
The Town of Mulgrave and the surrounding area is included because I suspect the Government recognized it had to do this, having not included it in the Bill in the first place. The Government alleged we had extensive consultations with every single person in Atlantic Canada, if you can believe it, before it put the legislation before the House. Yet all of a sudden it has to redefine Cape Breton Island in order to include the Town of Mulgrave. I think that town should be included in the programs offered to Cape Breton by this legislation. These are special programs recognizing the special needs of the island
April 27, 1988

population and, in this case, the Town of Mulgrave. Of course, in my riding in Newfoundland as well as that of the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) there are also towns and villages which are not included in these special provisions.
However, I want to be on the record as saying that when we as a legislative committee went to Cape Breton and held hearings in Port Hawkesbury, which is just on the Cape Breton side of the Canso Causeway, we had representations from the Town of Canso along with Guysborough and a number of other communities which are similarly industrially deprived, which have similar economic problems and difficulties in attracting industrial development to their region. The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) was there and welcomed the Mayor of Canso to the committee. He suggested to the Mayor that he hoped that when he, at an appropriate time, urged the committee to move in the direction of including Canso, he would gain the necessary support from the committee when the committee reported to the House to have that effected.
We came back to Ottawa and had a committee meeting here. In that meeting it was proposed, not by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso but by the Minister of Transport, to include only the Town of Mulgrave, which coincidentally happens to be the home town of the Hon. Member of Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso. It did not include the Town of Canso or Guysborough or any other little town or community along the way which had made representations to the committee. Then in committee it was suggested that the denial of unanimous consent at that stage was an attempt to deny to the people of Mulgrave the opportunity to participate in these industrial development benefits. That certainly was not the case.
You will see Motion No. 15, which was also ruled out of order for the same reason as Motion No. 14, because it tried, under the definition section, to expand the boundaries of the program. That motion repeats the motion now before the House. It also includes:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion presented to the House by my colleague from the constituency of Moncton in the great Province of New Brunswick which borders the Province of Nova Scotia, my home territory. More important, I want to appeal to all Members of the House, particularly Members from outside the Maritime provinces, to act to expedite the passage of this Bill.
I ask that of Members of the House of Commons because Bill C-103, which establishes the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, has been before this Chamber and committees of this Chamber for a sufficient time to allow all Members a full opportunity to consider the provisions of the Bill. It is now time to consider the interests of the people of Atlantic Canada. The purpose of this Bill, as explicitly stated under "Purpose" is:
-to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada
and, more particularly, to enhance the growth of earned incomes and
employment opportunities in that region.
All Members of this House have been through the evolution of economic initiatives by the Government of Canada. We saw the Department of Regional Economic Expansion change to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. I am sure that my colleague from Newfoundland will agree that everyone in Atlantic Canada was concerned that those Departments did not specifically deal with the special needs of the Atlantic area. Therefore, Members from Atlantic Canada requested the special consideration which has given rise to Bill C-103 for the creation of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
It grieves me that we are debating in the House of Commons changes to this Bill which will not be approved by the House of Commons and can only have the effect of delaying passage of the Bill, an adverse effect on all residents of Atlantic Canada. The time for review has passed and the time for action has come. It is impossible for me to believe that Members of the House of Commons from Atlantic Canada or any other part of Canada perceive that they are assisting the people of Atlantic Canada in their economic needs by delaying passage of this Bill. No Member can seriously suggest that he or she is acting in the interests of Atlantic Canadians by moving amendments to this Bill, which is a simple mandate for a new organization to assist in the economic development of Atlantic Canada and, in the case of the deprived island of Cape Breton and environs, the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
This Bill was only ever intended to establish a new vehicle for assisting Atlantic Canada in its economic expansion which has been delayed and deferred for many years by a national government which dealt with the Atlantic area through Departments of the Government which had other interests in other parts of Canada. We in Atlantic Canada have a chance to have our own agency with our own interests at its heart. Anyone who stands in this House and delays the process by

April 27, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
which that Agency is finalized, made operative, and placed in a position to answer the needs of Atlantic Canada, does a disservice to everyone in Atlantic Canada.
I cannot understand why my colleagues from Atlantic Canada are standing in the House at this hour of this day and further delaying passage of this Bill. I appeal to their better natures to put aside their silly political consideration, to put aside their delaying tactics, which they know will result in no better end than to deprive Atlantic Canadians of the opportunity to work under this new Agency, and to seek the ends which we all desire, that is, economic development for Canada.
In conclusion, I appeal to reason, I ask Members of the House from Atlantic Canada and those from outside Atlantic Canada to pass Bill C-103 to enact the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. When Hamilton's turn comes, I will be the first to stand in the House and assist Hamilton.

Mr. Speaker, it sounds like inverted logic to me, but I will proceed nonetheless.
The purpose of the last half of the Bill is to separate two aspects of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, the coal mining division and the industrial development division, such that the industrial development division of Cape Breton Corporation would now be under the aegis of Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, ACOA, while the coal division would carry on its activities without the integration of the over-all industrial development activities that had occurred in the last number of years.
We heard a great deal of thorough evidence on this Agency from Dr. Theresa MacNeil, Chairman of the Board of the Cape Breton Development Corporation, during our hearings in Port Hawkesbury.
The concern expressed by her and others privately to me was that to separate the two parts of Cape Breton Development Corporation from each other would amount to the destruction of a corporate culture that was working quite well for nearly 20 years. The integration of these activities were and still are a model for economic development as a result of using the assets turned over to the Cape Breton Development Corporation to create economic activity in Cape Breton, and using the ideas of the industrial development division to support economic activity in Cape Breton Island, and by using the expertise and the assets which remained as a result of the inevitable downsizing of some of the coal-mining activities. For example, when the fire at 26 Mine occurred, it was able to respond to the economic effects of the lay-offs that would become inevitable. The Cape Breton Development Corporation stepped in through
April 27, 1988

its industrial development division and used some of the assets that were left to create other economic activities and respond to those occurrences.
The entire organization, from the Board to the advisers and the community of Cape Breton, developed a great degree of faith in that organization and its ability to respond to the needs over the years.
While they were not always totally satisfied with it, like any other agency or arm of Government, it has performed very well on the whole.
The amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker) would completely stop that destruction of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. In fact, I proposed similar amendments in committee in order to delay this type of occurrence until it was certain that there would be no ill effects from such an action. I still believe that not enough consultation has taken place with the people of Cape Breton. The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), as well as the Senator from the other place who is the Minister responsible, have said there was extensive consultation about this issue all over Atlantic Canada. That is not the case with the Cape Breton Development Corporation. The Government had not even decided upon the definition of Cape Breton. It needed Royal Assent to redefine Cape Breton in order to include an area that is not even in Cape Breton.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) went to Port Hawkesbury and said he would urge the rest of the committee to include Canso, then returned to Ottawa and did nothing. This shows that it is quite obvious even he was not consulted when this legislation was put together. If he had been, presumably that representation would not have been made in Port Hawkesbury and he would have told the Mayor of Canso that the Government decided it would not include Canso.
While the rules of the House do not allow me to propose these amendments again, these amendments by the Member for Gander-Twillingate would allow the Standing Committee on Regional Industrial Expansion to do an evaluation after two years to see whether it needs to reverse this decision which the Government is presumably about to take.

Mr. Speaker, in keeping with my colleague's request, I will be brief. The amendments moved by the Hon. Member suggest the deletion of all the aspects that relate to taking Devco's Industrial Development Division into Enterprise Cape Breton and are unacceptable to the Government of Canada. The impression was given that there was no consultation and that this was just
April 27, 1988

something that came from somewhere in the annals of Government here in Ottawa. It was suggested by the Cape Breton Advisory Committee, chaired by Dr. Theresa MacNeil, who is now Chairman of Devco, in a report dated September of 1985 in which the Board identified certain matters as barriers to development caused by the confusion of a multiplicity of development agencies.
The Advisory Committee recommended two things. It recommended that a new development agency, Enterprise Cape Breton, independent in matters of policy, management and operations from the coal side of the corporation, Devco, be established. It also recommended that Enterprise Cape Breton should become a one-stop shop to the degree possible by encompassing the industrial development division of Devco and DRIE.
This committee recommended the very thing that is being put into effect in Bill C-103. The rationale behind the efforts contained in Bill C-103 is for better co-ordination of federal economic and industrial development activities in Cape Breton. It is designed to reduce duplication and overlaps. It is also designed to provide one-stop shopping in Cape Breton with regard to economic and industrial development.
As I mentioned before, it is consistent with the recommendations of the Cape Breton Advisory Committee. Adopting the amendments today would counteract all that is being worked on in order to provide that one-stop shopping atmosphere in Cape Breton.
With those comments we certainly recommend that these amendments be defeated.
